title: Transport and Communication
summary: Transport carries goods from areas of production to areas of consumption and from surplus to deficit areas, and moves people for jobs, education and emergencies. Communication keeps us informed and improves people's economic condition. Together they are called the lifelines of a country and its economy. Modes: land (roads, railways), water (inland, oceanic) and air (domestic, international).

Roads give door-to-door service, cost less to build and maintain, are cheapest for a few people and small loads over short distances, carry perishables like milk and vegetables quickly, link villages with towns and reach railway stations, airports and ports, and can be built in all terrains. By material they are metalled (pucca: concrete, cement, bricks, coal-tar) or unmetalled (kuchcha: mud, sand). By authority: village roads under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (about 80% of road length); district roads by the Zila Parishad (14%); state highways by the State Public Works Department linking state capitals with district headquarters (4%); National Highways by the National Highways Authority of India — only 2% of length but 40% of traffic; and border roads by the Border Roads Organisation for defence and border people.

Super highways built by NHAI: the Golden Quadrilateral linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata; the North–South Corridor from Srinagar to Kanyakumari; and the East–West Corridor from Silchar to Porbandar. The two corridors cross at Jhansi. The Grand Trunk Road built by Sher Shah Suri (16th century) is the oldest and longest; road length grew from 4 lakh km in 1947 to about 33 lakh km.

Railways are the cheapest way for thousands of people to travel long distances, with classes for all income groups and night journeys, and they carry bulky goods such as coal, cement, food grains, fertilisers and petroleum. Indian Railways started in 1853 from Bombay to Thane (34 km); today the network is over 64,000 km, the largest in Asia and fourth in the world, the largest government undertaking (1.6 million employees), divided into 16 zones, with its own budget. Blocking or burning trains (rail roko) causes huge loss and inconvenience.

Factors affecting railway density: relief (easy on flat land, difficult and costly in mountains, deserts, marshes, forests and flood-prone areas), agricultural productivity (the Gangetic plain — UP, Bihar, West Bengal, Punjab, Haryana — has a dense network), mining and industry, population density, and urbanisation. Hilly states like Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh have few railways. Modern facilities: Jammu–Kanyakumari direct link (3,751 km), diesel and electric locomotives, e-tickets and special freight wagons.

Water transport is the cheapest (no construction cost except maintenance), best for heavy and bulky goods and petroleum, fuel-efficient and eco-friendly. Inland waterways: about 14,500 km, of which only 3,700 km is navigable by mechanised boats. The Inland Waterways Authority of India (1986) manages National Waterways: NW-1 Ganga from Allahabad to Haldia (1,620 km), NW-2 Brahmaputra from Sadiya to Dhubri (891 km), NW-3 Kollam–Kottapuram canal in Kerala (205 km). Oceanic routes: India's coastline is 7,516 km; coastal shipping links 12 major and about 189 minor ports; international shipping carries most foreign trade. Major ports — west coast: Kandla (Gujarat), Mumbai and Jawaharlal Nehru (Maharashtra), Marmagao (Goa), New Mangalore (Karnataka), Kochi (Kerala); east coast: Tuticorin and Chennai (Tamil Nadu), Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Paradip (Odisha), Haldia and Kolkata (West Bengal).

Air transport in India began in 1911. It is the fastest mode, free from surface obstacles like mountains, forests and floods, vital for defence, connects continents, carries perishable and high-value goods, and helps during disasters; its drawback is high cost. Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd. serves ONGC, Indian Oil and the north-east. Major international airports: Indira Gandhi (Delhi), Chhatrapati Shivaji (Mumbai), Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose (Kolkata), Chennai (Meenambakkam), Kempe Gowda (Bengaluru), Rajiv Gandhi (Hyderabad); Srinagar is the northernmost and Amritsar serves Punjab.

Communication is a system of carrying messages to exchange thoughts, ideas and information. Personal communication: postal service (India's postal network is the largest in the world — about 1,55,000 post offices in 2001) and telephone/mobile. Mass communication: radio (began in 1927 from Mumbai and Kolkata; All India Radio reaches 98.8% of people), television (national service began in 1959; one of the biggest terrestrial networks), newspapers, cinema and satellites. Computers and IT are now the basis of communication and economic development. New technologies: internet, video conferencing, e-commerce, internet telephony, e-mail and tele-medicine have made the world a global village.

vsa: Explain two main factors affecting the density of railways.

(1) Relief: railways are easy and cheap to build on flat land, so the Gangetic plain has a dense network, while mountains, deserts and marshes have few lines. (2) Economic activity and population: areas with more agriculture, mining, industries, cities and dense population (UP, Punjab, West Bengal) have more railways.
How are 'rail roko' protests (train blockades) harmful for the nation and individuals?

They stop the movement of passengers and goods, causing great inconvenience, loss of business and loss of millions of rupees; burning coaches destroys public property built with years of effort and taxpayers' money.
What is the function of Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited? What is the drawback of air transport?

Pawan Hans, a government undertaking, provides helicopter services to ONGC and Indian Oil and to the north-eastern states. The drawback of air transport is its high cost, which keeps it out of reach of the common man.
Differentiate between personal communication and mass communication.

Personal communication is between individuals — letters, telephone, mobile, e-mail. Mass communication reaches a very large number of people at the same time — radio, television, newspapers, cinema and the internet.
Why are some states of India poorly connected by railways?

States like Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh have high mountains, rugged terrain, dense forests and heavy rain, which make railway construction very difficult and costly; low population and little industry also make it uneconomical.
sa: Analyse any three characteristics of road transport in India.

(1) Roads provide door-to-door service and link villages to towns, railway stations, airports and ports. (2) They are cheaper to build and maintain and are the most convenient for a few people and small loads over short distances, especially perishables. (3) They can be built in all terrains; they are classified by material (metalled/unmetalled) and authority (village, district, state, national highways, border roads).

or: Analyse any three characteristics of rail transport in India.

(1) It is the cheapest means for thousands of people to travel long distances, with coaches for every income group and berths for night journeys. (2) It carries bulky goods like coal, cement, food grains and petroleum. (3) It is the largest network in Asia (over 64,000 km), the largest government undertaking, divided into 16 zones, with modern facilities like e-tickets and electric locomotives.

sa: Analyse any three aspects of village roads.

(1) They link villages with each other and with main roads; they are built under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana. (2) They form about 80% of India's total road length. (3) They help farmers take produce to markets, give access to schools and hospitals and support rural development; many are still kuchcha and get damaged in rain.
How do roads contribute to the social and economic growth of a country? Explain three reasons.

(1) They connect rural areas with urban markets, helping farmers sell produce and perishables quickly. (2) They give access to schools, hospitals and jobs, and to railway stations, airports and ports. (3) They support trade, industry and tourism, and national highways and corridors speed up the movement of goods between big cities, saving time and fuel.
Why is there a dense rail network in the Gangetic plain but not in hilly and desert areas? Explain.

(1) The Gangetic plain is level, so railways are easy and cheap to build; hills and deserts make construction difficult and costly. (2) The plain is the food bowl of India and densely populated, so there is heavy movement of goods and people. (3) It has many large cities and industries, while deserts and hills have few people and little economic activity.
'From olden days till now waterways have been an important means of transportation.' Examine.

(1) It is the cheapest means as there is no construction cost except maintenance. (2) It is best for heavy and bulky goods — a ship carries lakhs of tonnes — and for importing petroleum. (3) It is fuel-efficient and eco-friendly; inland waterways (NW-1, NW-2, NW-3) reduce traffic on roads and ocean routes carry most of India's foreign trade.
Explain the importance of communication in our day-to-day life.

(1) It lets us exchange thoughts, ideas and information and share joys and sorrows with family and friends. (2) Radio, television, newspapers and the internet keep us informed about world events and help education and entertainment. (3) Mobile phones, e-mail, e-commerce, video conferencing and tele-medicine help business, banking and emergencies, making the world a global village.

la: Why are transport and communication called the lifelines of a country? Explain in six points.

(1) Transport carries raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets, helping agriculture, industry and trade. (2) It moves goods from surplus to deficit areas, especially perishables and food during shortages. (3) It lets people travel for jobs, education, health and tourism. (4) Roads, railways, waterways and airways together integrate the country and help defence and disaster relief. (5) Communication — post, telephone, radio, TV, internet — keeps people informed and connected and supports business, banking and governance. (6) Modern technologies (e-commerce, video conferencing, tele-medicine) speed up development and make the world a global village.
Explain the importance of air transport and of water transport for India.

Air: (1) the fastest means, covering hundreds of km in hours; (2) free from surface obstacles like mountains, forests and floods, so ideal for the north-east and remote areas; (3) vital for defence and disaster relief, and carries perishable and high-value goods; its drawback is high cost. Water: (4) the cheapest means with no construction cost; (5) best for heavy, bulky goods and petroleum imports and for most foreign trade through 12 major ports; (6) fuel-efficient and eco-friendly, and national waterways on the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Kerala canals reduce road traffic.
